claim: The authors report a learning-based predictive impedance-control architecture that switches between task- and safety-oriented impedance models, uses time scaling for predefined-time convergence, and learns a context-dependent meta-parameter. Under the evaluated models and disturbances, all predefined-time variants reduced final convergence error below 0.1 mm, while neural-network tuning achieved the highest composite reward. Passivity and safety remain conditional on low-level energy logic, switching, MPC feasibility, environment estimates, and time-scaling assumptions; the learned tuner itself does not establish passivity or human safety.
epistemic_status: peer-reviewed primary research with author-reported theory, simulation and limited physical case study
problem_and_setting: Physical interaction under varying environment stiffness, specified convergence deadlines and disturbances, followed by a human-arm ultrasound case study.
method_or_mechanism: Low-level MPC switches between task- and safety-oriented impedance models using interaction-force modeling and safety assessment. Energy-aware impedance variation supports the claimed passivity property, time scaling targets predefined-time convergence, and a contextual-bandit/UCB dataset plus neural network predicts meta-parameter g_nu from environment stiffness and specified convergence time. Training uses 10,000 simulations and 240 physical fine-tuning runs.
content_summary: Six controllers are compared across two models and no, step and continuous disturbances. PdT variants reportedly attain final error below 0.1 mm; NN tuning has the highest composite reward. Model A NN-PdT error is 0.000 for all disturbances and Model B is 0.030, 0.022 and 0.026. Reward combines error, extra force and maximum velocity, so it is not an independent safety metric. In ultrasound, three manual rewards were -11.254, -10.778 and -9.824 versus -9.557 for one NN trial; NN reported error 0, extra force 15.190 and maximum velocity 6.758 versus third manual 0, 15.638 and 6.642. The physical comparison is too small for repeatability or population claims.
synthesis_role: Evidence for combining model-based MPC/energy safety mechanisms with learned context-dependent tuning, distinguishing low-level conditional guarantees from tuner performance.
development_link: Connects predictive energy-aware impedance control with contextual-bandit collection and neural-network meta-parameter selection.

evidence.finding: MPC switches between task- and safety-oriented impedance models using real-time interaction modeling and safety assessment.
Passivity is attributed to impedance-variation energy logic and PdT convergence to time scaling.
UCB/NN tuning uses 10,000 simulations and 240 physical fine-tuning runs.
All PdT variants achieve final error below 0.1 mm and NN tuning has the highest tabulated reward; Model A errors are 0.000 and Model B 0.030/0.022/0.026.
Composite reward cannot be interpreted directly as passivity or human safety.
One NN trial scored -9.557 versus -11.254, -10.778 and -9.824 for three manual tunings.
One result per tuning condition does not establish repeatability or broad superiority.

boundary_conditions: Passivity depends on modeled energy logic, switching and force model.
PdT depends on time-scaling assumptions and feasible MPC.
Performance depends on environment estimation and contexts within training ranges.
The learned tuner does not independently prove passivity or safety.
Composite reward trades error, force and velocity.
Physical evidence is a small case study without ISO or clinical validation.
assumptions: Interaction force and environment stiffness are accurately estimated.
Time-scaling regularity and convergence assumptions hold.
Energy accounting remains valid across switches.

reported: IC, MPIC and no-PdT fail the reported below-0.1-mm target.
Default/manual g_nu obtains lower composite reward than NN tuning.
inferred: Learning itself does not prove passivity.
Main trial counts and uncertainty are unclear.
The ultrasound case cannot support broad human or clinical claims.
Higher composite reward may conceal force/velocity tradeoffs.
No ISO or clinical safety validation exists.
